query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Training a machine-learning-based interatomic potential on a strategically sampled ab initio dataset for both the solid and liquid phases of multicomponent alloys can substantially reduce the computational time required to accurately compute free energies and fusion properties (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD while retaining near-ab initio fidelity.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent alloys (high-entropy or concentrated solid solutions) in both crystalline and liquid states, sampled across a temperature range from ambient to just above their melting points.
generation.intervention: Fit and validate a machine-learning force field, trained on ab initio data that captures essential finite-temperature dynamics and electron–vibrational coupling, and then employ this ML potential to perform thermodynamic integration or molecular dynamics simulations for computing solid and liquid free energies.
generation.conditions: Employ a carefully selected training set of ab initio configurations spanning variations in temperature (room temperature to above melting) and composition, ensuring coverage of both solid and liquid regimes. Maintain a consistent representation of electronic contributions and anharmonic vibrations in the training data to preserve high-temperature thermodynamic relevance.
generation.structural_mediator: The machine-learning potential must capture near-ab initio force accuracy for both solid and liquid structures, providing physically meaningful interatomic forces across the melting transition and enabling free-energy evaluation.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential reproduces energies and forces from ab initio references, letting classical (or accelerated) simulations converge free-energy calculations at a fraction of the cost otherwise required by ab initio MD or TOR-TILD. The potential includes corrections for electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic contributions, ensuring faithful reproduction of temperature-dependent thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to pure ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, computational costs should decrease by at least one order of magnitude, while maintaining solid–liquid free-energy differences, fusion enthalpies, and transition temperatures within roughly 5–10% of ab initio results. This reduces time-to-solution and x100 cost while retaining predictiveness for high-temperature thermodynamics in multicomponent alloys.
generation.baseline: Performance comparisons to standard ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD on smaller binary or elemental systems will establish reference accuracy, quantifying deviations from benchmark free energies, entropies, and melting points.
generation.boundary: Applicability extends to moderately complex (up to five–six component) alloys and temperatures up to their liquidus region, though reliability for extreme temperatures or complex chemical interactions must be validated on a case-by-case basis.
generation.uncertainty: The method depends on the thoroughness of the ab initio training set. If the sampling strategy fails to capture critical regions of phase space (especially in the melt or near melting), or if electron–vibration coupling is modeled inadequately by the ML potential, larger errors can arise.

falsification_experiment.design: For a known multicomponent alloy with experimentally established fusion properties, generate a minimal ab initio dataset for both solid and liquid phases at multiple temperatures. The ML potential is fit to replicate these data. Then, predict solid and liquid free energies, fusion enthalpies, and melting temperature. Compare these values with direct ab initio MD, TOR-TILD data, and experimental measurements.
measurements: Solid and liquid free energies at key temperatures
Computational time for the entire workflow
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Significant deviation (>10% discrepancy) of fusion enthalpy or free-energy difference from the best available ab initio or experimental references, or failure to reproduce the correct melting point within 5–10%, would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractExploring the vast compositional space offered by multicomponent systems or high entropy materials using the traditional route of materials discovery, one experiment at a time, is prohibitive in terms of cost and required time. Consequently, the development of high‐throughput experimental methods, aided by machine learning and theoretical predictions will facilitate the search for multicomponent materials in their compositional variety. In this study, high entropy oxides are fabricated and characterized using automated high‐throughput techniques. For intuitive visualization, a graphical phase–property diagram correlating the crystal structure, the chemical composition, and the band gap are introduced. Interpretable machine learning models are trained for automated data analysis and to speed up data comprehension. The establishment of materials libraries of multicomponent systems correlated with their properties (as in the present work), together with machine learning‐based data analysis and theoretical approaches are opening pathways toward virtual development of novel materials for both functional and structural applications. This work introduced the high-throughput phase prediction of PtPd-based high-entropy alloys via the algorithm based on a combined Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA) and artificial neural network (ANN) technique. As the first step, the KKR-CPA was employed to generate 2,720 data of formation energy and lattice parameters in the framework of the first-principles density functional theory. Following the data generation, 15 features were selected and verified for all HEA systems in each phase (FCC and BCC) via ANN. The algorithm exhibited high accuracy for all four prediction models on 36,556 data from 9139 HEA systems with 137,085 features, verified by R2 closed to unity and the mean relative error (MRE) within 5%. chosen.why: A neural-network or Gaussian-process potential fitted to strategically sampled ab initio data can capture vibrational and electronic contributions at a fraction of the cost of explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD. Prior successes for simple alloys and elements show that ML potentials can accurately reproduce free-energy surfaces when trained on high-fidelity reference data, including critical anharmonic and electron–vibration effects. Benchmarking by comparing computed phase free energies and derived fusion properties (transition temperatures, enthalpies) with fully converged ab initio MD or TOR-TILD results will validate or refute the hypothesis. This approach is faster than ab initio and TOR-TILD, yet aims to maintain comparable fidelity, potentially enabling routine computation of high-temperature thermodynamics for complex, multicomponent systems.
